Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

[{"id": "arka-english-main-0-polish-long-0108", "row_sha256": "2737b76e32858a8b60754f1a93ca9c700d7d40cff96c4e710cffb8abf2901c87", "mode": "/polish", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Rewrite awkward phrasing into readable prose for the supplied profile, or plain prose when none is supplied. Preserve intent and certainty. Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "
we have been revising the bakery order form at juniper lane bakery since the first week of april, and this update covers the version staff began using on may 6. the old form was made for counter orders and then adapted for phone and web orders, which is why the same information showed up in different places and people sometimes missed it. the current work is to make the choices easier to follow without changing how an order gets prepared. the form is used by the front counter, the phone desk, and the person who checks the morning production list, so the changes have to make sense for all three. this is not a change to the bakery's prices or its pickup policy.

on the earlier form, customers could write a pickup date in a blank box, while the staff copy had a separate date field. if the two dates did not match, the person preparing the list had to ask which one was intended. the new form uses one pickup-date field, and the staff copy carries that date through automatically. the pickup time is still selected separately, in half-hour windows from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. orders for a time outside that range need to be discussed with a staff member; the form does not offer an outside-hours choice. the date field also displays the bakery's closed days so customers do not submit an ordinary pickup request for a day the shop is closed.

we moved the contact details closer to the top because people were reaching the cake options before giving a phone number. name and phone number are required for every order, but an email address is optional. the form accepts a phone number with spaces or dashes, and staff can read it from the printed copy without having to remove those marks. for web orders, the confirmation goes to the email address when one has been entered; if there is no email address, staff use the phone number for any follow-up. the form does not ask customers to create an account. that was left out because the bakery takes many orders from people who do not order frequently.

1. choices and notes

The first choice is the product type: bread, pastry, or cake. bread and pastry orders show a quantity box and a short notes box. cake orders open a separate set of choices for size, filling, and decoration. a customer can request a message on a cake, but the message field has a limit of  thirty characters so it fits on the printed kitchen slip. the examples beside that field now read “Happy 8th birthday, Mia” and “Congratulations, Lee,” rather than a longer example that made the space look unlimited. allergy information is entered in its own box, not in the general notes field. the form says that this box is for information staff need to review, and that entering an allergy does not by itself confirm that the bakery can meet the request.

we added a required choice for whether the customer wants the order packed as one item or split into separate packages. it appears for all product types because staff said the question comes up for bread and pastry orders as well as cakes. if the customer chooses separate packages, a second box asks how many packages are needed. the form accepts a number from two to twelve there. it does not let someone enter one, because choosing one item is already covered by the first choice. the packaging answer is copied onto the production list, but the number of packages is not printed on the customer receipt. staff wanted the production list to carry the detail and the receipt to stay short.

some customers used the general notes box to ask for a substitution, a later pickup, or a special decoration, even when the form had a specific choice for that request. the note below the box now says, “Use this space for details that do not have a separate choice above.” staff can still read and discuss a note, but writing something there does not change a selected pickup window or guarantee a decoration. for cake decoration requests, the customer must choose one of the listed decoration options first, then can add a detail in the notes box. if the requested decoration is not listed, the form directs the customer to call the bakery before submitting the order. this is intended to reduce unclear requests, not to prevent a customer from asking a question.

we checked the form using six sample orders: two bread orders, two pastry orders, and two cake orders. one cake order included a message at the full thirty-character limit, and the message printed on one line on the kitchen slip. another sample had no email address, and the confirmation screen still showed the phone number as the contact method. in the first pass, a staff member could not tell whether “three” in a package note meant three total packages or three additional packages. the separate package-count box now labels the number as the total number needed. the staff member checked that wording on the revised test form, and said the distinction was clear. these were test orders entered by staff, not customer orders, and they did not test whether an allergy request could be accommodated.

at the counter review, Nia said, “I can find the pickup date without checking the paper copy now, but I still want the phone number where I can see it.” the phone number remains near the top of the form, directly under the customer name. she also asked if the decoration list could use shorter names, because two choices wrapped onto a second line on the tablet. we shortened “seasonal buttercream flower arrangement” to “seasonal buttercream flowers” and kept “simple border” as it was. the shorter label fits on one line on the tablet used at the counter, while the printed form still shows the full selected choice in the order details. no decoration choices were removed. the front-counter staff checked the wording, but the bakery has not yet reviewed the labels with its cake decorator.

the production list now groups orders by pickup date and then pickup time, instead of sorting them by the time the order was entered. staff requested that change because a late-entered morning order had appeared below orders for the afternoon on the old list. the customer receipt continues to show the order details in the order they were entered, and does not use the production-list sorting. for phone orders, the person taking the call reads the selected product, quantity, pickup date, pickup time, and packaging choice back to the customer before saving the form. for web orders, customers see those details on the confirmation screen. staff can correct an entry before saving a phone order; a web customer who spots a mistake after submitting needs to call the bakery. the form does not provide an edit link after submission.

the current assessment is limited to whether the revised form presents the existing order choices clearly and carries the entered details onto the staff materials described here. in the six staff-entered sample orders, the date, time, product, quantity, and packaging choices appeared in the expected places, and the tested cake message fit on the kitchen slip. the packaging count wording was changed after the first pass, and the revised wording was checked by one staff member. the test does not establish that customers will interpret every label as intended, that requested decorations or allergy needs can be met, or that the form handles order volumes beyond the six samples. the bakery will use the form for counter, phone, and web orders as described above; the assessment does not cover payment processing or any change to prices or pickup policy.", "output": "We have been revising the bakery order form at Juniper Lane Bakery since the first week of April, and this update covers the version staff began using on May 6. The old form was designed for counter orders and later adapted for phone and web orders. As a result, the same information appeared in different places, and staff sometimes missed it. The current work is intended to make the choices easier to follow without changing how an order is prepared. The form is used by the front counter, the phone desk, and the person who checks the morning production list, so the changes need to work for all three. This is not a change to the bakery’s prices or pickup policy.

On the earlier form, customers could write a pickup date in a blank box, while the staff copy had a separate date field. When the dates did not match, the person preparing the list had to ask which one was intended. The new form has one pickup-date field, and the staff copy carries that date through automatically. Customers still select a pickup time separately, in half-hour windows from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Pickup times outside that range need to be discussed with a staff member; the form does not offer an outside-hours choice. The date field also displays the bakery’s closed days so customers do not submit a standard pickup request for a day the shop is closed.

We moved the contact details closer to the top because people were reaching the cake options before providing a phone number. A name and phone number are required for every order, but an email address is optional. The form accepts phone numbers with spaces or dashes, and staff can read them from the printed copy without removing those marks. For web orders, the confirmation goes to the email address if one has been entered. If not, staff use the phone number for follow-up. The form does not ask customers to create an account. We left that out because many bakery customers order infrequently.

1. Choices and notes

The first choice is the product type: bread, pastry, or cake. Bread and pastry orders show a quantity box and a short notes box. Cake orders open a separate set of choices for size, filling, and decoration. Customers can request a message on a cake, but the message field is limited to thirty characters so it fits on the printed kitchen slip. The examples beside the field now read “Happy 8th birthday, Mia” and “Congratulations, Lee,” instead of a longer example that made the space seem unlimited. Allergy information goes in its own box, not in the general notes field. The form says this box is for information staff need to review, and that entering an allergy does not by itself confirm that the bakery can meet the request.

We added a required choice asking whether the customer wants the order packed as one item or split into separate packages. It appears for all product types because staff said the question comes up for bread and pastry orders as well as cakes. If the customer chooses separate packages, a second box asks how many are needed. The form accepts a number from two to twelve. It does not allow someone to enter one, because the first choice already covers a single item. The packaging answer is copied onto the production list, but the number of packages does not appear on the customer receipt. Staff wanted the production list to include the detail while keeping the receipt short.

Some customers used the general notes box to ask for a substitution, a later pickup, or a special decoration, even when the form had a specific choice for that request. The note below the box now says, “Use this space for details that do not have a separate choice above.” Staff can still read and discuss a note, but writing something there does not change a selected pickup window or guarantee a decoration. For cake decoration requests, customers must first choose one of the listed options and can then add a detail in the notes box. If the requested decoration is not listed, the form directs customers to call the bakery before submitting the order. This is intended to reduce unclear requests, not to prevent customers from asking questions.

We checked the form using six sample orders: two bread orders, two pastry orders, and two cake orders. One cake order included a message at the full thirty-character limit, and it printed on one line on the kitchen slip. Another sample had no email address, and the confirmation screen still showed the phone number as the contact method. During the first pass, a staff member could not tell whether “three” in a package note meant three packages in total or three additional packages. The separate package-count box now labels the number as the total number needed. The staff member checked the revised test form and said the distinction was clear. These were staff-entered test orders, not customer orders, and they did not test whether an allergy request could be accommodated.

During the counter review, Nia said, “I can find the pickup date without checking the paper copy now, but I still want the phone number where I can see it.” The phone number remains near the top of the form, directly under the customer’s name. Nia also asked whether the decoration list could use shorter names because two choices wrapped onto a second line on the tablet. We shortened “seasonal buttercream flower arrangement” to “seasonal buttercream flowers” and kept “simple border” as it was. The shorter label fits on one line on the tablet used at the counter, while the printed form still shows the full selected choice in the order details. No decoration choices were removed. Front-counter staff checked the wording, but the bakery has not yet reviewed the labels with its cake decorator.

The production list now groups orders by pickup date and then pickup time, rather than sorting them by the time the order was entered. Staff requested this change because, on the old list, a late-entered morning order appeared below afternoon orders. The customer receipt continues to show order details in the order they were entered and does not use the production-list sorting. For phone orders, the person taking the call reads the selected product, quantity, pickup date, pickup time, and packaging choice back to the customer before saving the form. For web orders, customers see those details on the confirmation screen. Staff can correct an entry before saving a phone order. A web customer who spots a mistake after submitting needs to call the bakery; the form does not provide an edit link after submission.

The current assessment is limited to whether the revised form presents the existing order choices clearly and carries the entered details onto the staff materials described here. In the six staff-entered sample orders, the date, time, product, quantity, and packaging choices appeared in the expected places, and the tested cake message fit on the kitchen slip. The packaging-count wording was changed after the first pass, and one staff member checked the revised wording. The test does not establish that customers will interpret every label as intended, that requested decorations or allergy needs can be met, or that the form handles order volumes beyond the six samples. The bakery will use the form for counter, phone, and web orders as described above; the assessment does not cover payment processing or any change to prices or pickup policy."}]
